extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematically-inclined philosophers, and mathematicians interested in mathematical practice and foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the quality, naturalness, and research value of mathematical definitions and concepts (e.g., when a stipulative or revised definition is 'proper' or 'natural'). Focuses on practice-driven epistemic and metaphysical considerations illustrated by cases like the Legendre symbol and quadratic reciprocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as research objective / proper definition counts as advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians often set finding the ‘right’/‘proper’/‘correct’/‘natural’ definition as a research objective, and success—finding ‘the proper’ definition—can be counted as a significant advance in knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat discovering or refining definitions as substantive mathematical achievement (as in algebraic geometry). Use historical examples where redefinitions signaled progress. Assess whether the proposed definition played a role in advancing understanding, proofs, or theory-building rather than merely renaming existing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness (significant consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper definition is fruitful when it supports ‘trivial’ results that have ‘significant consequences’ and contributes to addressing salient 'why?' questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the definition yields consequences considered significant (not merely trivial logical consequences). Example: Spivak's claim that properly defined terms make theorems 'trivial' in an illuminating way; the Legendre symbol compresses case distinctions and streamlines proofs. Use explanatoriness as a benchmark: does the definition help answer why phenomena hold?

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical naturalness (carving at the joints)
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is mathematically natural if it 'carves mathematical reality at the joints' rather than being an arbitrary or merely pragmatic convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on surface syntax alone to judge naturalness; investigate substantive mathematical behavior, relations to deeper theory, and how the concept figures in mathematical practice. Example: the Legendre symbol is judged natural because later theory (class field theory/Artin reciprocity) shows it arises naturally. The verdict that a concept is natural is itself a mathematical question supported by technical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification (compression of cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable definition can unify disparate cases into a single uniform statement or reduce many separate cases to fewer ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the unification is genuine and illuminative rather than spurious. Example: Dirichlet's use of the Legendre symbol reduces Gauss's eight cases to two. Beware anti-patterns: unification produced by gerrymandered/disjunctive predicates (e.g., 'x is a milkshake or Saturn') is unilluminating. Philosophical literature (Kitcher) warns that only projectible/unified patterns count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power / supports 'natural proofs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer definitions that enable or support proofs which explain why a theorem is true (not merely provide verification); mathematicians seek 'natural' proofs that give understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the definition helps produce proofs that reveal underlying reasons (Gauss's demand for natural proofs; many proofs of quadratic reciprocity sought for explanatory depth). Explanatory success often motivates the acceptance of a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to generalize / facilitation of fruitful reformulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good definition facilitates reformulation and generalization to broader domains and deeper theories (e.g., extensions that lead to class field theory or Artin reciprocity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the definition is adaptable to larger contexts and whether it points toward more general structures. Example: pursuit of reciprocity laws led from quadratic reciprocity to higher reciprocity and eventually Artin reciprocity; the Legendre symbol appears naturally as a special case of the Artin symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical well-behavedness (experience-tested indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators such as multiplicativity, periodicity, being a homomorphism/surjective map between natural groups, and yielding Abelian structure are signs that a function or definition is 'well-behaved'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List and check technical properties appropriate to the domain: for the Legendre symbol, complete multiplicativity, periodicity mod p, and that restricted maps are surjective homomorphisms were cited as markers of naturalness. Such properties are experience-tested heuristics that the concept is mathematically robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projectibility / inductive support
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural mathematical property is one that supports correct inductive reasoning (projectibility); mathematical induction and enumerative induction play roles in conjecture and discovery (Euler's conjecture about quadratic reciprocity is an example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the property yields reliable inductive inferences and plays the role analogous to 'projectible' predicates in empirical induction. Note the philosophical point that successful mathematical induction does not depend on physical causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: disjunctive/gerrymandered definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions that are disjunctive or contrived to force unification (gerrymandered predicates) are suspect because they may produce spurious unification without genuine explanatory or structural content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when a unification is achieved only by packing unrelated cases into a disjunction (the 'milkshakes or Saturn' example). Such definitions should be treated skeptically unless further mathematical structure shows they are non-artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role in identifying intended interpretations under underdeterminacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A naturalness judgment helps single out 'intended' interpretations in cases where several meanings or formalizations are underdetermined by data or theory (one of the functions listed in Lewis' catalogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use criteria of naturalness, simplicity, similarity, and explanatory fit to decide between competing formalizations; examine whether mathematical practice treats one interpretation as privileged (historical examples and reformulations like Dedekind's).

rubrics_metrics.name: Status as object of study (self-consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the function or property introduced by a definition becomes itself an object of mathematical investigation is a relevant criterion: if so, that supports its mathematical significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether mathematicians study the introduced function systematically (e.g., the Legendre symbol's many studied properties). If the function generates rich theory, that is evidence the definition is substantive rather than a mere linguistic convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/practice-based corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgments about a definition's merit are grounded in historical developments, the resulting body of mathematics, and practice (proofs, reformulations, successful generalizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the historical trajectory: did the definition lead to fruitful lines of inquiry (Gauss, Dedekind, Hecke, Hilbert)? Use the accumulation of successful theory-building and cross-connections across subfields as corroborating evidence for accepting a definition.
